claims.text: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr can be synthesized by powder-metallurgy routes.
Powder-metallurgy HfNbTaTiZr specimens typically contain approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The relevant powder-metallurgy specimens have a typical fine-grained microstructure.
A model explicitly incorporating oxygen-defect and phonon scattering will improve conductivity predictions for HfNbTaTiZr.
The improvement will apply in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Oxygen atoms are incorporated into the HfNbTaTiZr crystal lattice.
Lattice-incorporated oxygen locally disrupts the periodic potential and acts as an electron-scattering center.
Oxygen-induced scattering reduces electron mean free paths.
Defect scattering dominates electron transport in approximately 1 wt.% oxygen HfNbTaTiZr from 0 to 200 K.
Oxygen defects produce significant residual resistivity at low temperature.
Both phonon and oxygen-defect scattering are significant from 300 to 1200 K.
Combined phonon and defect scattering leads to a moderated increase in conductivity at high temperature.
The proposed model will reproduce a low-temperature residual-resistivity plateau.
The proposed model will reproduce a tempered temperature-dependent increase in high-temperature conductivity.
Conventional defect-free analytical models overestimate HfNbTaTiZr conductivity because they neglect defect scattering.
The proposed model will significantly reduce prediction discrepancies relative to conventional defect-free analytical models.
The asserted applicability is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr near 1 wt.% oxygen and the intervals 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Applicability at substantially higher oxygen contents or from 200 to 300 K is unverified.
Defect clustering, microstructural heterogeneity, and processing-dependent defect distributions may alter the oxygen-scattering contribution and model universality.
A low-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr comparison specimen can be produced using suitable powder-processing methods.
